opus-5.5.text:
Good question. In a pure Transformer, positional encoding has to do a lot of work, because softmax attention is permutation-invariant. Without something like RoPE, the model has no built-in sense of order. Hybrid architectures change that picture quite a bit.

In something like Kimi Linear, most layers are linear attention. Kimi Delta Attention is a gated DeltaNet variant. These layers are recurrent by construction. They process tokens in order, and the decay and gating mechanisms already give you a strong, learnable notion of recency and position. You could almost say the linear layers act like a learned positional encoding for the whole network. Given that, the global attention layers don't really need to carry positional information themselves. So the Kimi team chose NoPE for their MLA layers, and I think that's a very reasonable choice.

There's also a practical benefit, especially for long context. RoPE has well-known problems when you extrapolate beyond the training length. That's why people keep adjusting the base frequency and using tricks like YaRN or NTK scaling. With NoPE in the global layers, a lot of that headache goes away. The global layers become something like pure content-based retrieval: "find the token that matches what I'm looking for, wherever it is." That's exactly the role you want them to play in a hybrid. The linear layers handle local, order-sensitive structure, and the full attention layers handle precise long-range lookup. Decoupling those roles is clean. And with MLA, dropping RoPE also simplifies things, since you no longer need the separate decoupled RoPE dimension trick that DeepSeek introduced.

Qwen3-Next took a more conservative path. As far as I understand, they kept RoPE in the gated attention layers, applying it to only part of the head dimension. I don't think that's wrong either. RoPE is very well understood, it's battle-tested at scale, and partial RoPE leaves some dimensions free for position-agnostic matching. It's a kind of middle ground. When you're shipping a flagship model, there's a lot of value in not changing too many things at once.

My personal view is that the field is moving toward NoPE, or at least much weaker positional encoding, in the global layers of hybrids. Order information really belongs in the recurrent part of the model. That said, it's still an empirical question. There's some evidence that NoPE layers can be a bit worse at certain fine-grained positional tasks, and at very long lengths their attention can become diffuse. You might need things like attention-logit scaling or careful normalization to keep them sharp. So I wouldn't call it settled. But conceptually, I find the NoPE-plus-linear-attention combination quite elegant. It lets each component do what it's good at.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the field is moving toward NoPE or weaker positional encoding in hybrid models’ global layers, identifying a trend toward less RoPE use.

r002.rationale: The candidate states that RoPE has problems when extrapolating beyond training length and that using NoPE in global layers avoids much of that difficulty.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that in a hybrid architecture the choice matters less than people assume, and the reason is that the linear or recurrent layers are already doing most of the positional work for you.

If you look at Kimi Linear, the global attention layers use NoPE, and that was a deliberate decision. Once you have Kimi Delta Attention or Gated DeltaNet style layers interleaved every three or four layers, those recurrent layers are inherently causal and position-aware. The state is built up sequentially, so the representation flowing into the full-attention layer already carries a strong implicit notion of order. Adding RoPE on top of that becomes somewhat redundant. And removing it buys you something concrete: NoPE attention layers tend to extrapolate more gracefully to sequence lengths beyond the training window, because you are not baking in a rotational frequency schedule that was tuned for a particular context length. That matters a lot when the whole point of the hybrid is long context.

Qwen 3 Next went the other direction and kept RoPE on the global attention, and I think that is also defensible. RoPE gives you a very reliable recency bias at the attention level, and in practice it helps with training stability and early convergence. If your recurrent layers are not quite strong enough, or if you have a smaller ratio of linear to full attention, the inductive bias from RoPE is something you do not want to give up. There is also an engineering argument: the entire inference and training stack around RoPE is extremely mature, with YaRN and other extension tricks that people already know how to use.

My own view is that if the linear layers are doing the heavy lifting on local structure, then NoPE for the global layers is the cleaner design. You are essentially making a division of labor: the recurrent layers handle positional and local information with their natural causal decay, and the full-attention layers are there for precise, content-based retrieval over the entire context, where you actually do not want a strong positional prior interfering. A retrieval head ideally cares about what the token is, not how far away it is.

The caveat is that NoPE can be a bit more sensitive during training. Early in pretraining the model has to learn to extract position from the recurrent layers, and sometimes you see a slightly slower start. Some teams address that with partial RoPE, applying rotation to only a fraction of the head dimensions, which is a reasonable middle ground. So I would not say one is strictly correct. I would say NoPE is where I think the design is headed as the linear components get stronger, and RoPE is the safer choice if you are not yet confident in that.

r001.rationale: The response favors NoPE as linear components strengthen, but describes Kimi Linear using NoPE and Qwen 3 Next retaining RoPE. It does not identify a shared trend across hybrid architectures toward reducing RoPE usage.

r002.rationale: The response says NoPE layers extrapolate more gracefully beyond the training window because they avoid a rotational frequency schedule tuned to a particular context length, communicating that RoPE may hinder length extrapolation.

astra-6.text:
I’d frame it as a question of what the global attention layers need to contribute. In a hybrid architecture, the linear or recurrent layers already carry information about sequence order. So a global attention layer without explicit positional embeddings—NoPE—isn’t necessarily operating on position-free representations. Its inputs can already contain that information.

That makes NoPE an interesting choice if you want global attention to focus on retrieving relevant content across a long context. RoPE gives attention an explicit positional structure, which can help when relative location matters, but it also introduces positional behavior that you have to manage when extending the context length.

I wouldn’t say one is universally better. The useful question is whether explicit position in the global layers adds something the other layers aren’t already providing. I’d compare them under the same training setup and look separately at content retrieval, order-sensitive tasks, and performance beyond the training context length. For architectures like Kimi Linear and Qwen 3 Next, the choice really needs to be evaluated together with the rest of the hybrid design.

r001.rationale: The response compares RoPE and NoPE and calls NoPE interesting, but does not identify a shared trend toward reducing RoPE usage.

r002.rationale: It says RoPE introduces positional behavior that must be managed when extending context length, suggesting it can make length extension harder.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d frame it in terms of what the global attention layers need to contribute. In a hybrid architecture, some layers already handle local context or carry information forward through a recurrent state. Global attention can then focus on retrieving information that those layers don’t preserve well.

RoPE gives that retrieval an explicit positional structure. That’s useful when relative distance and order matter, but it also makes behavior at longer context lengths depend on how the positional encoding generalizes. NoPE removes that explicit positional constraint from the attention scores, which can be attractive for content-based retrieval. It doesn’t necessarily mean the model has no positional information: the causal mask and the surrounding layers can still make its representations sensitive to order.

So my intuition is that NoPE is a reasonable choice when global attention mainly serves as a content lookup mechanism, while RoPE is useful when those layers also need to reason directly about positional relationships. But I wouldn’t infer a universal winner from Kimi Linear or Qwen 3 Next alone. You’d want a controlled comparison with the same training setup, checking both retrieval and order-sensitive tasks across context lengths. The important question is how the global layers complement the rest of the architecture.

r001.rationale: The response compares RoPE and NoPE but does not identify a shared trend toward reducing RoPE usage in hybrid attention architectures.

r002.rationale: It says longer-context behavior depends on how positional encoding generalizes, but does not clearly state that RoPE may hinder length extrapolation.
